source: Matorina & Poppenk (2019 preprint) REM negatively predicts statistical learning but not other forms of gist
finding: Large preregistered test of four gist types over one week. Only inferential gist (transitive inference) held up. Category gist, summary gist and statistical learning decayed.
numbers: N=69 (30 men, 38 women, 1 other); tests same evening, next morning, day 7. Category gist fell 22%, instance memory 15%, detail 6%. Inferential gist rose 0.6% while premise pairs fell 2%. Category gist time effect F(2,182)=38.72, p<.001.
limits: Preprint, not peer reviewed. Single task per gist type. Overnight EEG scoring had only moderate rater agreement for SWS.
agent_relevance: Overlap alone is not enough to keep a generalisation. Only relational structure where every item links to every other survived. A merge step should keep rules that form a connected relational set and expect isolated summaries to decay.

source: Matorina & Poppenk (2019 preprint) REM negatively predicts statistical learning but not other forms of gist
finding: Slow-wave sleep did not predict any gist type. This fails to replicate the SWS prediction of Lewis and Durrant (2011) and Durrant et al. (2011) for statistical learning.
numbers: SWS proportion did not predict inferential gist, statistical learning, summary gist or category gist. SWS vs summary gist trend only: b=1.625, t(56)=1.980, p=.053. NREM vs statistical learning b=.445, p=.041 (not FDR-significant, threshold .013).
limits: Exploratory NREM effects fail multiple-comparison correction. Time of day and lab differ from the original.
agent_relevance: The core IOtA claim (SWS replay of overlapping traces builds gist) lacks a clean large-sample confirmation. Do not build the agent's merge step on the claim that more replay equals more gist.

source: Matorina & Poppenk (2019 preprint) REM negatively predicts statistical learning but not other forms of gist
finding: More REM predicted worse statistical learning, the opposite of a gist-building role for REM.
numbers: Proportion REM vs statistical learning controlling for time: b=-0.626, t(58)=-2.662, p=.010 (survives FDR). Total sleep time negatively predicted summary gist: b=-0.343, p=.015 at post-sleep (not FDR-significant).
limits: Correlational. Authors suggest REM discretises (separates) memories rather than merging them.
agent_relevance: Two opposing processes may exist: merge and separate. An agent that only merges rules will lose the distinctions a separating process would keep. Keep an exceptions list beside any merged rule.

source: Matorina & Poppenk (2019 preprint) REM negatively predicts statistical learning but not other forms of gist
finding: Authors conclude memory overlap is an insufficient condition for long-term generalisation.
numbers: Structured relational sets (each item related to all others) were enhanced; triplet-structured statistical sequences and category sets, which also overlap, were not. Test-retest effect for deterministic sequences from triangles: t(44)=-2.09, p=.043.
quote: memory overlap is an insufficient condition for long-term generalization
limits: Interpretation by the authors, from one design.
agent_relevance: Merging rules should be gated on structure, not just on surface overlap between rules.

source: Ellenbogen, Hu, Payne, Titone & Walker (2007) Human relational memory requires time and sleep
finding: Transitive inference improved after 12 hours that included sleep, mostly for the most distant pair (B>E). Wake did not help that pair.
numbers: N=56. 20-min group n=12; 12-h n=31 (sleep n=14, wake n=17); 24-h n=13. B>E inference: 54% at 20 min; 93% after sleep, 69-70% after wake (t(29)=2.21, p=.03); 86% at 24 h. One-degree B>D about 73-75% in both groups (t(29)=0.18, p=.86). Sleep-by-degree interaction F(1,27)=7.3, p=.01. Averaged inference sleep 79% vs wake 72% was not significant (p=.51).
limits: Between-subject, small cells (14 vs 17). Effect only on the far pair; the averaged effect was null. Page text was read through a summarising fetch tool, not the PDF.
agent_relevance: Support for far-inference gains from offline integration, but fragile and small. An agent test: after consolidation, check derived two-step conclusions, not one-step ones.

source: Lerner & Gluck (2019) Sleep and the extraction of hidden regularities: a systematic review and the importance of temporal rules
finding: Across about 68 study units, sleep effects on hidden-rule extraction are mixed. Explicit rule detection benefits appear mainly for temporal rules.
numbers: Explicit detection in NRT/SRTT paradigms: 14 of 30 studies found an effect. Temporal rules: 31 of 45 showed some sleep effect; stationary: 15 of 22. All 9 experiments on explicit detection of stationary rules found no sleep benefit. Weather Prediction Task: 3 of 5 positive. ASRT: no effect in four studies. Categorization/generalisation split about evenly.
limits: Vote-count review, no pooled effect sizes (reports none). I read the first 100,000 characters only, via a summarising fetch.
agent_relevance: The sleep literature does not show a general merge benefit. Benefit depends on rule type. For the agent, test merge on sequence-like rules separately from static ones.

source: Lerner & Gluck (2019) review
finding: Documented failures: no sleep benefit in several gist and generalisation studies, including older adults.
numbers: Null or absent effects listed: Song 2007, Nemeth 2010, Hallgato 2013, Csabi 2014 (ASRT); Hennies 2014; Kemeny & Lukacs 2016; Robertson 2004; elderly samples (Spencer 2007; Pace-Schott & Spencer 2013); Schapiro 2017; Lutz 2017 (no immediate effect); Ashton 2018 (no immediate effect, effect at one-week relearning).
limits: Listed from the review's table via a summarising fetch; the original papers were not opened.
agent_relevance: Publication record is not uniformly positive. Treat the replay-builds-gist story as a hypothesis with a mixed track record.

source: Newbury & Monaghan (2019) When does sleep affect veridical and false memory consolidation? A meta-analysis
finding: No overall effect of sleep on false memory (a gist-like intrusion) or on accurate memory in DRM word-list studies.
numbers: Lure words, sleep vs wake: Hedges g=.129, SE=.210, 95% CI [-0.282, 0.539], p=.540. Without the one unpublished study: g=.165, p=.469. Heterogeneity Q(12)=63.227, p<.001 (13 effect sizes). Egger test p=.365 (no sign of publication bias).
limits: DRM is only one gist paradigm. Nap and overnight both included.
agent_relevance: A direct hit on the simplest claim that sleep strengthens gist. Gist gains, if real, depend on task features, so the agent should not assume merging helps by default.

source: Newbury & Monaghan (2019) meta-analysis
finding: Moderators: sleep raised false recall but not false recognition; list length also moderated the effect.
numbers: Recall studies: g=0.606, SE=0.299, 95% CI [0.020, 1.192], p=.043. Recognition studies: g=-0.150, SE=0.243, p=.538. Number of words per list was a significant moderator (Q(2) test).
limits: Moderator cells are tiny, so estimates are imprecise. Recall effect barely excludes zero.
agent_relevance: Gist intrusions show up when the model must produce (recall) rather than pick (recognise). In an agent, merged rules may cause false generation errors, not false recognition errors. Check with generation tests.

source: Lutz, Diekelmann, Hinse-Stern, Born & Rauss (2017) Sleep supports the slow abstraction of gist from visual perceptual memories
finding: Sleep did not change gist at 10 hours but improved gist after one year. Item memory was gone at one year.
numbers: N=28 analysed (20-min group n=15; 10-h group n=13). 17 returned after a mean 386 days (9 and 8). At 10 h sleep enhanced episodic-like old-shape memory, not prototype (gist) memory. At one year prototype knowledge present only if slept after encoding. Gaze time on prototypes correlated with prototype memory in sleepers, r=0.57, p=0.025.
limits: Tiny sample, with 11 of 28 lost to follow-up. Gist did not correlate with SWS or REM from the experimental night (all |r|<0.34).
agent_relevance: Gist benefit may need many cycles and a long delay. Short-term merge checks may miss it; schedule consolidation over many tasks, not one.

source: Lewis & Durrant (2011) Overlapping memory replay during sleep builds cognitive schemata
finding: Information overlap to abstract (IOtA) theory: repeated replay of overlapping traces strengthens the shared elements; SWS downscaling weakens the non-shared ones.
numbers: Not read this session. Secondary description only (via the Matorina paper and a search summary). Europe PMC lists 357 citations.
limits: Opened false; no numbers taken from the original paper.
agent_relevance: Direct source for the merge-overlapping-rules idea. Open the paper before relying on any detail.

source: Durrant, Taylor, Cairney & Lewis (2011) Sleep-dependent consolidation of statistical learning
finding: Reported as the main support: SWS duration correlated with improvement on a statistical learning task.
numbers: Not read. Described in Matorina & Poppenk as SWS duration correlating with statistical learning improvement.
limits: Opened false. Not replicated by Matorina & Poppenk (SWS did not predict statistical learning).
agent_relevance: Founding human evidence for IOtA; later weakened by the larger null.

source: Nagel et al. (2026) preregistered online replication of Diekelmann et al. (2010) on sleep and false memories
finding: Reported as a failed replication of the overall sleep effect on false memories.
numbers: Not read. A search summary says no overall sleep effect; more false memories after sleep only when intrusion-adjusted performance was high.
limits: Opened false. URL is a placeholder; details come from a search snippet only.
agent_relevance: Another sign that the sleep-gist effect is conditional on performance level.

source: Ellis et al. (2020) DreamCoder: growing generalizable, interpretable knowledge with wake-sleep Bayesian program learning
finding: Alternating a search phase with a sleep phase that refactors solved programs into a shared library gave large gains. This is the closest computational model of overlap-to-abstraction.
numbers: SyGuS: 3.7% solved before learning, 79.6% after (10-min budget); best prior synthesiser CVC4 82.4%; DreamCoder 84.3% with a generous budget. In LOGO graphics and tower building no alternative solves more than 60% of held-out tasks; DreamCoder nearly 100%. Learns 93% of laws and identities after 8 wake-sleep cycles in physics.
limits: Not an LLM (neural recogniser plus enumeration). Takes about a day on 20-100 CPUs. Ablating either abstraction or dreaming hurt.
agent_relevance: Direct template for a subgoal library: merge repeated sub-programs after each batch, then re-solve. Both abstraction and a learned search guide were needed.

source: Ellis et al. (2020) DreamCoder
finding: Authors map their abstraction phase to slow-wave sleep and the dreaming phase to REM, but state the biology link is speculative.
numbers: Compression objective: choose library edits that minimise description length of programs found while awake.
quote: we speculate that our approach could bring wake-sleep learning algorithms closer to the actual learning processes
limits: Authors say neither DreamCoder nor the Helmholtz machine is a biological model.
agent_relevance: The compression criterion (does a merge shorten solutions) is a measurable test for any merge in our agent.

source: Grand et al. (2024) LILO: Learning interpretable libraries by compressing and documenting code
finding: Merging code into a library with Stitch compression hurt a GPT solver until each abstraction got a readable name and docstring (AutoDoc).
numbers: Naive Stitch abstractions changed solve rate by -30.60 (REGEX), -2.91 (CLEVR), -11.11 (LOGO). AutoDoc gave +9.73 (REGEX), +2.27 (CLEVR), +0.00 (LOGO). Final test tasks solved (max): REGEX 93.2 vs DreamCoder 45.6 vs LLM solver 90.0; LOGO 73.87 vs 36.94 and 41.44. Mean across 3 seeds: REGEX LILO 77.07 vs LLM solver 76.13.
limits: Mean-level gains are small on REGEX (77.07 vs 76.13, std 14). 3 seeds only. On LOGO AutoDoc added nothing; semantic errors.
agent_relevance: Merged rules must be named and described in words or the model misuses them. A merge without a clear label can cut accuracy by tens of points.

source: Stengel-Eskin, Prasad & Bansal (2024) ReGAL: refactoring programs to discover generalizable abstractions
finding: A code bank of shared helper functions, built by refactoring over batches and pruned, raised accuracy of several LLMs without training.
numbers: Gains of 11.5% on LOGO, 26.1% on date understanding, 8.1% on TextCraft (best cases). CodeLlama-13B with abstractions beat GPT-3.5 without by 19.2% on LOGO. Random curriculum ordering cut LOGO by 18.7%. Under distribution shift: +3.6% over baseline, pruning +3.5%, editing on new data +2.3%, total 9.4%. Gains seen with as few as 25 demos (+2.56%) and nearly half the set (+8.45%).
limits: Not every domain has reusable abstractions; gains smaller for strong models; learned abstractions differ from human ones. Numbers are maxima over models and domains.
agent_relevance: Supports a bank with pruning and ordered easy-to-hard feeding. Pruning alone helped, so merging needs a delete step.

source: Wang, Mao, Fried & Neubig (2024) Agent Workflow Memory
finding: Inducing reusable workflows from past successful runs and adding them to memory lifted web agents. Online induction from the agent's own runs also worked.
numbers: Relative success rate up 24.6% on Mind2Web and 51.1% on WebArena. Mind2Web cross-task step success: 36.2 (baseline) to 45.1 offline, 43.6 online. Cross-domain: 18.6 to 32.6 offline, 35.5 online. Gap widens as train-test distance grows (8.9 to 14.0 absolute points). Beats human-written workflows by 7.9%.
limits: Action F1 sometimes dropped (cross-task 60.6 to 57.3). Wrong workflows degrade the model; some websites' training and test tasks differ. GPT-4 only.
agent_relevance: Best match for merging overlapping rules into subgoals. Needs a success filter: only induce from runs that passed a check (G2/G3).

source: Suzgun, Yuksekgonul, Bianchi, Jurafsky & Zou (2025) Dynamic Cheatsheet
finding: A self-curated memory of strategies and code let a model reuse and refine insights across questions. Gains depended on model strength.
numbers: Claude 3.5 Sonnet +27% on AIME 2024 and +30% on AIME 2025. GPT-4o on Game of 24: about 10% to 99% by reusing stored Python. GPQA-Diamond +9% for Claude. Claude 3.5 Haiku GPQA: baseline 43.4, DC- 41.9, DC-Cu 43.7, DC-RS 49.0; AIME 2025 0.0 to 13.3.
limits: GPT-4o-mini gains were small or negative (AIME 2024: DC-Cu and DC-RS below baseline). o1 and DeepSeek R1 gave minimal or inconsistent gains. Flawed stored heuristics can stall or degrade performance.
agent_relevance: Gains are large when reuse is a code or recipe, small for weaker models. Memory curation cannot make up for weak base capability; gate the library by model strength.

source: Lin et al. (2025) Sleep-time compute: beyond inference scaling at test-time
finding: Computing offline on a context before queries arrive cut test-time compute and amortised over related queries.
numbers: About 5x less test-time compute for the same accuracy on Stateful GSM-Symbolic and Stateful AIME. More sleep-time compute: up to +13% (GSM) and +18% (AIME). Multi-query: cost per query down 2.5x. Efficacy tracked how predictable the query was from the context.
limits: Authors' own tasks were modified to be stateful. Helps less when queries are unpredictable.
agent_relevance: Offline consolidation pays when later questions share structure with earlier ones. Predictability from context is a usable trigger for running consolidation.

source: Zhao et al. (2024) ExpeL: LLM agents are experiential learners
finding: Extracting natural-language insights across many trajectories helped, and the source of gains differed by task.
numbers: Insights-only vs retrieval-only: 36% vs 31% (HotpotQA) and 50% vs 55% (ALFWorld). Randomly selected examples 40.0 vs ExpeL 48.5 in one ablation. Hand-crafted insights beat ReAct but trailed LLM-written insights; adding reflections to insight generation hurt. Better base LLMs gave better insights.
limits: Table cells partly garbled in text extraction; numbers cross-read from prose. Gains differ by environment.
agent_relevance: Cross-trajectory generalisation helps knowledge-style tasks; raw trajectories help action-style ones. Keep both, and do not feed failure reflections into the merge.

source: Cross-source pattern across the LLM library papers (DreamCoder, LILO, ReGAL, AWM, Dynamic Cheatsheet, ExpeL)
finding: Every system ran its merge on solved examples with some check, and every one reported a failure case: unlabelled abstractions, weak base models, wrong workflows, or domains with no shared structure.
numbers: Failure sizes seen: -30.60 points (LILO REGEX, unlabelled abstractions), 18.7% drop with random ordering (ReGAL LOGO), GPT-4o-mini below baseline (DC), action F1 down 3.3 points (AWM cross-task).
limits: This is my synthesis of the six opened papers, not a separate study.
agent_relevance: Rules for the schema: merge only checked-successful items, label each merged rule, order easy to hard, prune, and measure against the plain model (G7).

source: Lutz et al. (2017) Sleep supports the slow abstraction of gist
finding: Rival account: gist abstraction needs multiple nights, not one. Short-term tests would miss it.
numbers: Abstract states gist abstraction is thought to need multiple nights; the 10-hour test showed no sleep effect on gist while item memory gained; one-year test showed gist only after post-encoding sleep.
limits: One group tested the one-year effect on 17 people; no multi-night manipulation was run, so the multi-night idea is untested here.
agent_relevance: Do not judge a library merge from a single batch; track the library over many tasks.

source: Suzgun et al. (2025) Dynamic Cheatsheet
finding: Memory built by a stronger model did not reliably help a weaker one.
numbers: Authors report mixed results when transferring memory across models; a smaller model lacking capacity to read the strategies can stall or degrade. R1-style models gave minimal or inconsistent gains because solutions were too verbose.
limits: Described as ablation observations; exact numbers not given in the text I read.
agent_relevance: A shared rule library must match the reader model's ability. Test the library on the target model, not the one that wrote it.

source: Stengel-Eskin et al. (2024) ReGAL
finding: Order of material fed to the merge step mattered a lot.
numbers: Replacing the easy-to-hard curriculum with random ordering dropped LOGO accuracy by 18.7%. Retrials helped build more useful helper functions and more demos.
limits: One domain reported in the text lines I read.
agent_relevance: Feed the merge simple, checked cases first; merge on a random order risks bad abstractions.
